profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at a mid-size SaaS company preparing an internal 'state of the practice' initiative on software effort estimation. The team wants to produce a reusable package for engineering leadership before annual planning starts: a literature-backed summary of current estimation approaches, a lightweight survey of internal teams, and a recommendation memo about what estimation practices the company should adopt or stop using. The immediate meeting is between the engineering manager sponsoring the work and the staff engineer coordinating execution. Their agenda is to define what will be produced over the next three weeks, who owns each part, how the internal survey and review will be run, and what 'ready for leadership review' means. The expected outcome is an agreed plan for the deliverables, timeline, and division of work for the estimation-practices review.

members.name: Priya Nair
members.expertise: Engineering operations, planning processes, cross-team coordination, delivery reporting
members.background: Priya manages the developer productivity group and has spent the last four years standardizing planning rituals across product teams; before that she was a technical program manager at a larger enterprise software company.
members.private_state: She wants a concise package that leadership can quickly consume before quarterly planning kickoff, and she is trying to avoid creating a research-heavy effort that slips or requires broad executive coordination.
hidden_assumptions: A 'survey' means a short internal questionnaire to current engineering managers and tech leads, not a broad external industry instrument.
A 'literature review' means a curated practical synthesis of a manageable set of high-signal sources rather than an academically exhaustive review.
The 'recommendation memo' is a leadership-facing decision brief with clear actions, and appendices or raw material are secondary.
When something is 'ready for review,' it should be polished enough to circulate to directors without caveats.
Using the standard planning spreadsheet and existing delivery metrics is the default way to gather any supporting internal data.

members.name: Lucas Chen
members.expertise: Software process measurement, developer tooling, empirical studies in engineering practice, internal analytics
members.background: Lucas leads measurement initiatives for the engineering effectiveness program and previously completed a part-time master's thesis on empirical software engineering methods.
members.private_state: He wants the work to be methodologically credible enough to influence future process changes, and he is concerned that a too-shallow summary will repeat folklore without exposing causal drivers behind effort variation.
hidden_assumptions: A 'survey' means a structured study instrument with role segmentation, comparable questions, and enough responses from ICs and managers to support patterns.
A 'literature review' means a systematic pass over recent and classic estimation research with explicit inclusion criteria and traceable notes.
The 'recommendation memo' should be evidence-backed and accompanied by supporting analysis artifacts that others can inspect later.
When something is 'ready for review,' it can still be an expert draft intended for feedback before leadership circulation.
If they are examining current practice, they will pull data from Jira issue histories and estimation fields rather than rely mainly on manager recollection.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'run a survey of current estimation practice.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya means a brief internal pulse survey sent to about 12 engineering managers and tech leads, mainly to gather directional input quickly.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Lucas means a more formal internal study across managers and individual contributors, with segmented responses and enough sample diversity to compare practices.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In software organizations, 'survey' naturally covers both a quick stakeholder questionnaire and a more structured study; because both are talking about internal practice and both assume speed matters, neither feels a need to define the term.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to include a 'literature review' as part of the package.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya assumes this includes roughly 10-15 well-known papers, industry reports, and a concise synthesis of practical methods relevant to planning decisions.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Lucas assumes this includes a systematic review of academic and industry sources from the last decade plus foundational work, with explicit screening, categorization, and traceable references.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both think a literature review obviously involves reading prior work and summarizing it; the disagreement is about completeness and documentation standards, which feels like execution detail rather than a separate planning decision.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the package should be 'ready for review' by the end of the second week.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya means polished, narrative-complete, and safe to send directly to directors as the near-final version.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Lucas means a technically coherent draft with caveats, open questions, and supporting notes, suitable for expert feedback before leadership sees it.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Teams often use 'ready for review' as shared project shorthand, and both are imagining a reasonable intermediate milestone; the hidden difference is the standard of completeness and audience, which usually remains implicit.

misalignment_points.topic: How internal evidence will be assembled
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'ground the recommendations in our own delivery data.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya assumes Lucas will use the existing planning spreadsheet, forecast-vs-actual summaries, and manager-supplied examples because those are already compiled and low-friction.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Lucas assumes he will extract Jira history and estimation-field data to reconstruct estimation behavior at issue and epic level, then use interviews only as interpretation support.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both think they are simply agreeing to use internal evidence, and each defaults to the data collection method most normal in their role; since neither method changes the headline objective, it slips by as an unspoken implementation assumption.

turns.inner_thought: I need this to land as a practical package leadership can absorb quickly before quarterly planning ramps. Three weeks is already tight, so I want a concise set of artifacts: a crisp summary, a lightweight input gather, and a decision memo that doesn't spiral into a research program. If we keep it bounded and polished, I can socialize it with directors without extra coordination overhead.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I want to use the next three weeks to put together a practical package on software effort estimation that leadership can use before annual planning starts. The goal is something grounded enough to be credible, but streamlined enough that it actually helps decisions.

turns.inner_thought: That framing works as long as 'practical' doesn't become superficial. I want to organize this around three evidence layers: what teams currently do, what the literature says, and recommendations tied back to observed behavior. For internal evidence, I should pull Jira issue histories and estimation fields early; otherwise we'll end up relying on recollections. And the literature review needs to be substantive enough to separate real drivers of effort variation from cargo-cult estimation rituals.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I can structure it around current practice here, evidence from the literature review, and recommendations tied to how teams actually estimate work. If we do that well, the package should be useful both for planning and for any follow-on process changes.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I should keep reinforcing that this is meant to stay lightweight. By literature review I mean a curated, high-signal synthesis, not a thesis. And the survey of current estimation practice should be quick: a short questionnaire to the managers and leads who already know the planning motions. That should give us enough directional input without creating a giant coordination task.
turns.utterance: My instinct is that we keep it fairly concise: a literature review plus a survey of current estimation practice, and then we turn that into a decision-oriented recommendation memo. I want the whole thing to stay lightweight and focused on what leaders should do differently.

turns.inner_thought: Agreed in principle. For the survey of current estimation practice, I want questions that let us compare responses by role so we can see where perceptions diverge. And for the literature review, I want to cover causal effort drivers, uncertainty sources, and estimation contexts, not just methods for improving estimate accuracy. If we don't do that, the recommendations will be too shallow to change anything.
turns.utterance: Yes, that works. I’d especially want the survey of current estimation practice to capture where different roles are experiencing the process differently, and the literature review should help us explain the drivers behind effort variation, not just list techniques people use.

turns.inner_thought: He's aligned on the overall shape, which is good. For internal evidence, we should use what already exists: planning spreadsheets, forecast-versus-actual summaries, and a few manager-supplied examples. I can get managers to provide those quickly. That gives enough grounding without asking for bespoke data work.
turns.utterance: I also want us to ground the recommendations in our own delivery data. The managers can probably give us examples pretty quickly of how estimates are being done today, which should help us anchor the picture of current practice.

turns.inner_thought: Great, then I have permission to start pulling the data immediately. I'll query Jira histories and estimation-field patterns so we can reconstruct how estimates changed over time and compare actuals against planned work. The manager examples will be useful context, but I don't want them to be the primary evidence base.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I can pull the internal data early so the recommendations are anchored in what our teams have actually done, and then we can use the examples to help interpret what we’re seeing.

turns.inner_thought: I need a strong milestone at the end of week two. By then, I want a polished package that I could comfortably put in front of directors, with the last week reserved for small edits and rollout prep, not major restructuring. If that slips into an exploratory draft, we'll miss the planning window.
turns.utterance: On timing, I’d like us to work toward the package being ready for review by the end of the second week. That would leave the third week for minor edits, packaging, and getting it ready to roll out.

turns.inner_thought: Week-two ready for review is reasonable if that means a solid expert draft: synthesis in place, recommendations drafted, notes traceable, and a few caveats still open for feedback. I can have the core analysis assembled by then, even if I’m still tightening support artifacts before broader circulation.
turns.utterance: Yes, I can work to that. By the end of week two, I should have the synthesis and draft recommendations assembled so it’s ready for review, and then we can use the last week to tighten anything that comes back.

turns.inner_thought: I'll keep ownership lines simple. Lucas can handle the survey and literature review; that's his lane. I'll handle stakeholder alignment and shape the recommendation memo into the leadership-facing decision brief. Appendices or backup material can exist, but the main thing has to be crisp and easy to consume.
turns.utterance: Why don’t we split it this way: you own the survey and the literature review, and I’ll handle stakeholder alignment and the framing of the recommendation memo. That should keep the execution moving while I make sure the final package lands with the right audience.

turns.inner_thought: That division works. I'll start by drafting a proper instrument for the survey, building a source list for the literature review, and outlining the analysis plan for the internal data pull. Then I can connect those findings into the recommendation memo so the claims are inspectable later and not just polished assertions.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I’ll start with a question set and a source list this week, then connect what we find in the internal data back into the recommendation memo so the recommendations follow from the evidence.

turns.inner_thought: I should reinforce the audience one more time. Directors need something they can scan quickly and act on. Once it's ready for review, I plan to put time on calendars and circulate it without a lot of caveats. That means I need confidence the package reads cleanly and doesn't feel like work-in-progress.
turns.utterance: Perfect. The main thing I’ll keep pushing on is that the output needs to be easy for directors to consume. Once it’s ready for review, I’ll block time on the calendar and start lining up the leadership conversation.

turns.inner_thought: Okay, next step is to make the workstream legible. I'll circulate an outline, the preliminary instrument for the survey of current estimation practice, and an evidence plan covering the internal data extraction and analysis path. That should let us get feedback early while I continue building toward the week-two review draft.
turns.utterance: Great. I’ll circulate an outline, a preliminary instrument, and an evidence plan in the next couple of days so we can make sure the timeline still holds and I can get moving on the core work.
